To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the oil thickness estimation from remotely sensed data is challenging because oil water spatial/spectrals contrasts are affected by multiple factors and the oil water spectral contrasts are not always linear with oil thickness, and that a multistep approach is proposed to estimate oil thickness.

the oil water spatial and optical contrasts are affected by oil thickness, emulsion state, and optical properties of oil-covered water, and these contrasts can be used to classify the type of oil (emulsion and/or nonemulsion) and estimate the relative oil thickness.

the interpretation of oil water spatial/spectra contrast is complicated because of the effects of sun glint strength and the emulsification state of oil, and because of the spatial resolution of the sensor and the oil thickness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interpretation of oil water spatial/spectrals contrasts, which are important for the estimation of oil thickness and the development of algorithms to map oil slicks.
understanding the spatial/spectral oil water contrasts, which are important for the detection and estimation of oil thickness in remote sensing images.
the challenges of interpreting oil water spatial and temporal contrasts for the estimation of oil thickness, which is important for oil spill response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
oil water spatial and spectrals contrasts are highly variable and depend on several factors, which makes it difficult to estimate oil thickness accurately using remote sensing imagery.
oil water spatial/spatial contrasts are not always consistent and are not always related to oil thickness.

oil water spatial and optical contrasts are complex and difficult to quantify, but that the use of multiple remote sensing techniques and data sets can help improve our understanding of the spatial and spectral contrasts of various oil spills and the associated challenges.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

optical remote sensing is capable of detecting oil in the surface water, and the detection of oil thickness is possible, yet more research is needed to better understand and interpret the spatial/spectral oil water contrasts.
oil water spectral contrasts are complex and variable.
oil water spatial and/or spectral contrasts are not a direct measure of oil thickness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oil water spectral contrasts are highly variable and depend on the oil type, sun glint strength and the optical properties of the underlying water.
oil thickness is a key variable in interpreting oil water spatial/spectra contrasts, and it can be estimated from remote sensing data.
oil thickness can be estimated from remotely sensed spectra of oil slicks, but the accuracy of the estimation is limited by a number of factors.
